"Give me Shelter"

By: Jacqui Jayamaha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Statistics show that Durban has approximately 4000 Homeless people living on the street or in Shelters. What is being done for these destitute citizens by the City claiming to be the Most Caring in

Unique Selling Point:
Durban, touted by the Safer Cities wing of the Municipality as an International Tourism Mecca and "The most liveable and caring City in SA" has an ugly truth in plain sight for those who care to see it, as approximately 4000 homeless people live on the streets or in filthy Shelters, where they are exploited and often abused. Despite fantastic research on the Homeless in the City that was tabled, bought to council and passed in 2016 nothing has been done in 2 years. We investigate why promises to improve the lives of Durban's destitute have not been fulfilled and who is responsible for this total neglect of citizens and their basic human rights.

Summary:
We take a real look at the lives behind the faces of destitute homeless folks in Durban. We spend the day with Homeless woman Serena Bather who wants to share her story with us. From riches to rags, she will show us where she once lived in an upmarket Durban suburb and then to her old haunts and places she slept on the streets, on the beach and under bridges.
We go undercover into some of the worst shelters in SA and see how the Homeless are forced to live in filthy places they pay for per night for. Often exploited these folk have lost all hope of a better life and more importantly their dignity. We will see where little children are raised among drug lords and sex workers, born into a web they often never escape.
We confront the Municipality and talk to NGOs about thier on going efforts to help these people from their marginalised situations to gain some sort of momentum to claw their way out from this horror of an existence.

Press Release:


Durban’s Homeless Shelters
Over 4000 homeless people in Durban rely on the Ethekwini Municipality to provide them with meals and a safe shelter for the night. But often these shelters are far from a place of safety. Carte Blanche goes deep undercover into some of the dismal shelters to expose how the homeless and vulnerable are exploited, abused and forced to live in filthy conditions.


Script:


INSERT: “Give me Shelter” KZN
PRODUCER: JACQUI JAYAMAHA
PRESENTER: DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER
TX DATE: 5 AUG 2018
DURATION: 10 minutes

V/O Durban is promoted internationally as one of South Africa’s major tourism hubs with its subtropical climate and beautiful beaches.
Devi Link “Despite romantic perceptions of this coastal metropolis, there exists a bitter reality - Durban’s approximately 4000 Homeless people. Seen as a scourge, they are the ostracized urban inhabitants of grimy alleys, cold pavements and quasi ‘Shelters’.
V/O 45-year old Serena Rader used to live in Durban’s upmarket suburbs, but a few bad decisions rendered her homeless.
Serena “My first month on the street I was humiliated, I didn’t want to look at myself, I felt dirty, I felt worthless. You know people have no respect for you.
V/O It can take hours of begging at traffic lights or dancing for the possibility of a few Rands – just to have something to eat and a safe place to sleep. Sometimes there’s not enough even then.
Devi Link Homeless people have just two accommodation options – it’s either the streets or the so-called Shelters.
Andrew “For my knowledge with shelters, shelters are for people like me, not for kids, most of the time the conditions are terrible. They got fleas, you got lice, you got rats, you know rodents running around and that’s a health hazard”.
V/O Andrew Devipursad has been living in various shelters for 10 years.
Andrew: “You don’t know who, you’re living with, thieves you’re living with thugs. And the owners, who ever runs the shelter, they don’t pay much attention to that.
V?O Durban has approximately 24 privately owned shelters. Sources told us that downtown, the infamous Pickering Street, is littered with shelters with some of the most inhumane conditions. We sent undercover operatives to various shelters.
V/O The air hits you with the strong stench of crack cocaine and urine. A massive fire hazard, dingy corridors are made of plywood and lead off to family rooms. There are huge adjoining warehouse dormitories.
V/O Tenants are packed together on double bunk beds with bed bug ridden mattresses.
Andrew You don’t know who slept on that bed, whether the sheets were changed or not. You just need that shelter, and that’s just for the night.
V/O Men, women and children share ablutions and blocked toilets are surrounded by trash and excrement.
V/O All this at a cost of around R40 per person per night or R180 for a small family room. **(blurred all recognisable faces)
Serena: “Us homeless don’t like to talk because we need the cheaper shelters…so we’ll l put up with the abuse and all of that because they need it.
V/O The municipality has been derelict in devising a strategy to provide regulated housing for the homeless, resulting in a growing need for low cost accommodation. For this reason private, unregulated shelters are mushrooming all over the city – so if you have a building you can start a shelter, as simple as that!
V/O This blatant exploitation is extremely lucrative: About 750 people are living in the 6 shelters on this block. We estimate that altogether, these shelters have the capacity to bring in R720 000 per month. With no maintenance evident, where is the money going to?
V/O Ahmed Gora Arbee is the registered owner of some of the buildings which house shelters. But when we called him for an interview, he claimed he couldn’t hear us on the phone. Hours later, his attorney sent Carte Blanche an email alleging that a foreign national had in fact hijacked Arbee’s building. He further claimed his client wasn’t receiving any rental income and currently owes the municipality over a million Rand in unpaid rates and taxes. **(documents highlighted and then brought forward with drop shadows)
So who exactly was collecting the money? Days later our producer confronted the man in charge.
Emmanuel - Wait Wait wait wait baba sorry sorry wait, explain what’s going on!
Wait, wait, wait
(Prod) I’m trying to explain what’s going on, we busted wanted to find whose running this business, because we know inside it’s not good, it’s very bad, there’s no electricity, theatre the toilets are broken, your’e the manager?
Emmanuel Yes I can’t explain.
(Prod) So how much money do you make a month?
Emmanuel Like I said I can’t explain you all
(Prod) All the homeless people how much are they paying a month?
Emmanuel Like I said I can’t explain you all who the owner for this place, how much they pay, I can’t explain you all
(Prod) But we heard you were getting all the money everyday?
Emmanuel Yes it’s true
(Prod) How much do you thinK?
Emmanuel Like I say I can’t, tell you all of you, I can’t explain you all!
(Prod( R100s thousand?
Emmanuel - I can’t explain you all R100?
(Producer) - Who takes all the money?
it you that get’s the money? How much do you get? Thousands?
Emmanuel Ya it me that takes the money!
(producer) The conditions are
Emmanuel”I can’t tell you”
V/O Human rights activist Raymond Perrier says these conditions are barbaric.
Raymond I worked in a refugee camp in Uganda where the conditions are better than 2.6kms from the City Hall in Durban.
Perrier runs the Denis Hurley Centre, where an interfaith community feeds over a thousand homeless people each week, offering showers, clean clothes and a free clinic. He says the responsibility for Durban’s homeless lies squarely with the municipality.
Raymond “The city has a responsibility to take care of people who are marginalised in the community, they have the obligation to provide social work support to people in need.
V/O This informal settlement in Dalton Road is within walking distance of the Mayor’s office. This is the site the Municipality selected for relocation of the homeless. We discovered a large group of people living – literally – in a sewer.
Devi Link “The Municipality is responsible for the welfare of all its citizens, so what is the Ethekweni municipality doing to ensure that the homeless have access to the basics?
V/O Deputy Mayor Fawzia Peer’s portfolio is responsible for the marginalised and destitute.
Fawzia “The municipality has developed a strategy, Because each pillar has er, a job to be done, like human settlements or possibly the social issues so one cannot really….erm…no.
V/O In 2016, the municipality had commissioned a study on the homeless and their needs, to the tune of R1.600.000. But none of the research seems to be informing the Deputy Mayor’s understanding of the lives of people in their care.
Fawzia - Firstly what they do in the morning, they come out from the places that they live, in the pipes or under the bridges or the railway tracks, they would go to the beachfront, have a nice shower there and then go to Denis Hurely and have a nice meal there er, a very appetizing meal daily that’s provided, and then you go back and you sleep, you know, in the rail tracks.
Devi “Are you happy with that?”
Fawzia I don’t think that’s a very good thing, I would say sometime, it’s beyond out control, because there’s a large flow of people coming in” …“We also have er, these other shelters that are owned privately and most of them use those shelters as well”.
V/O Despite the homeless being Peer’s portfolio, she had no first-hand knowledge of their living conditions.
Devi “And maybe part of the problem is that they’re not regulated, so I can start up a shelter tomorrow, charge whatever I want, How do you feel about that?”
Fawzia “Well you know I feel strongly for the homeless that are using those shelters and they’re not in good condition and I think we have to look at that”.
Devi “Is there any way that the City can use resources that you already have to go in and have a look?”
Fawzia “We do have, I mean staff, going around, possibly, but er, I didn’t get anything in writing from them that the conditions are bad and that we need to do something about it “.
V/O Peer had not been briefed on the progress of the city’s Dalton Road project, where the Interfaith NGO community has picked up the slack to provide at least some basic services.
Devi I’ve been told that homeless people were moved from Albert Park to Dalton Road and that was that. It was just a bare piece of land is that true?
F I think we moved homeless people from Albert Park simply because we wanted to use the park
Devi There’s no ablution facilities there.
F We have to look at it now.
Devi “In terms of the City’s 2016 report that was commissioned by the City, what has come out of that report?
****Fawzia “We did the research, we did bugger all! Can I tell you that!
V/O While the municipality fumbles, its NPOs like Ashley Hewitt’s ‘Turning Point’ that have to pick up the pieces.
Ashley Nobody grows up wanting to be homeless; nobody grows up saying I want to be destitute someday and yet they find themselves in incredibly difficult circumstances and unfortunately there aren’t a lot of people doing enough to help these guys.
Serena Everyone needs a home, everyone needs love, no one can say it will never happen to me coz you never know. Give us dignity, give the country dignity.
